archetype.name: Pocket Passer (vertical-leaning)
archetype.definition: A rhythm thrower from the pocket who rarely runs. This year he has pushed the ball into tight windows and down the field far more often, and that is where most of his value comes from.

report.headline: More aggressive Stroud is trading completions for chunk plays, and it's mostly working
report.take:
Stroud's fourth season looks a lot like his best football so far, reached a different way. His completion rate (62.8%) sits right at the league average of 62.5% and ranks 31st. Yet he is third in passing yards per game at 273.6, his EPA per dropback beats the qualifier average by 0.154, and his adjusted net yards per dropback rank 10th. The gap between those numbers is the story. His aggressiveness, the share of throws into tight coverage, has jumped to 20.63% from 12.8% last year. He is giving up easy completions to hunt bigger ones.

The depth splits show the payoff. Throws of 10+ air yards return 0.397 EPA a play. Everything under 10 returns 0.096, and passes behind the line actually cost the offense 13.4 EPA across 35 attempts. Deep balls (20+) carry 0.498 EPA with a +6.9 CPOE, which is real accuracy downfield, not just volume. The intermediate area is the odd one: a -7 CPOE but 0.341 EPA and 8 TDs, so the throws he does complete there are doing heavy lifting. Protection is helping. Houston's offensive hit rate ranks 4th, his pressure rate ranks 9th-lowest, and his sack rate of 5% beats the league's 7.9%. His career profile has always been a pocket player who holds the ball near three seconds, so this is the same quarterback with the leash taken off.

The numbers flatter him in a couple of places. He has thrown 16 TDs on 43 red-zone attempts with a +14.6 CPOE there. His last three games show a 9.9% TD rate against a 57.4% completion rate and a -5.6 CPOE. That combination does not hold: touchdowns are outrunning the underlying accuracy. His 0.9% INT rate (9th) is also light for someone throwing into this many tight windows, and it has already crept to 2% over the last three. Against Cleveland he went 20/38 with a 31.6% aggressiveness rate and a 3.3-second time to throw, and still produced three scores on 0.1 EPA. The target tree is lopsided too. Xavier Hutchinson has drawn 54 targets at 0.065 EPA apiece, while Jaylin Noel (0.721) and Kayshon Boutte (0.445) have been far more efficient on far fewer looks.

Where this goes: the yardage and downfield efficiency look like a real, coached change rather than a hot streak. The 2024 dip (-0.007 EPA per play, 12 INTs) is the cautionary version of an aggressive Stroud, but this year's turnover-worthy count is low and his bad-throw rate is down 3.4 points from last year. Expect the touchdowns to cool and the interceptions to tick up. The per-play value should hold in the top half of the league, with weekly swings driven by how often the shots land.

strengths.title: Downfield throws drive the offense
strengths.body: His throws of 10+ air yards produce roughly four times the per-play EPA of his short game, and his deep accuracy is above expectation rather than lucky. The jump in aggressiveness is a deliberate shift from last season, and the deep CPOE says he can carry it. That makes it the most sustainable part of his profile.

strengths.title: Clean pockets, few sacks
strengths.body: His sack rate is well under the league average, and over his last five games it has dropped to 2.9%. Houston's line ranks among the best at keeping hits off him, which gives the slower-developing vertical concepts time. His pressure-to-sack rate (26.2%) is in line with his career, so this comes from protection rather than a change in his habits. It holds as long as the line stays intact.

strengths.title: Efficient to the right and middle
strengths.body: Throws to the right side return 0.31 EPA with a +7.3 CPOE, and the middle 0.373. That is where the offense lives. It reads like a play-design and timing strength he can lean on weekly.

concerns.title: Touchdowns outrunning his accuracy
concerns.body: His last three games show a 9.9% TD rate alongside a 57.4% completion rate and a -5.6 CPOE. His red-zone line (16 TDs, +14.6 CPOE) is also hotter than any quarterback holds over a full season. Some of his scoring will come back toward his yardage.

concerns.title: Interceptions are the price of aggression
concerns.body: A season INT rate of 0.9% is low for someone throwing into this many tight windows. It has already doubled over the last three games. This is a cost of his strength rather than a decision-making flaw, but expect more picks than he has so far.

concerns.title: Dead weight in the quick game
concerns.body: Screens and throws behind the line have cost the offense 13.4 EPA, and the left side runs at a -7.2 CPOE. The volume to Hutchinson has returned almost nothing per target, while Noel and Boutte have been far more productive on fewer looks. This is mostly scheme and distribution, and it is fixable, but it drags his efficiency below what his downfield play deserves.

trend.note: He started slowly with negative EPA in Weeks 2-3, then had a strong run from Week 4 to Week 9: 12.8, 8.9, 12.4 and 15.1 EPA games around a 1.1 against the Giants. Cleveland was a near-zero 0.1 on 20/38. The last five are his best stretch (0.216 EPA per dropback), but the completion rate has wobbled.

nextGame.headline: Big-favorite Thursday rematch with a banged-up Colts secondary
nextGame.body:
Indianapolis held him to 167 yards and -2.5 EPA back in Week 3. This defense is mid-pack against the pass, though, and gives up explosive passes at the second-highest rate in the league, which suits his vertical approach. The coverage breakdown is uneven. Throws to the opponent's WR2 have been shut down, while WR3s and tight ends have feasted, which points to Noel, Boutte and Dalton Schultz rather than a forced feed to the second receiver. The bigger caveat is game script. Houston is favored by 11.5 and the Colts' offense ranks last in passing EPA. Opponents run on Indy more than usual, so a lead could flatten his volume in the second half. That said, his EPA when leading by 9+ has been strong on a small sample.

Availability tilts toward Houston. Colts corners Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward are both questionable after leaving Sunday's game, on a short week. Losing either would thin the coverage he has to throw into. Indy is also missing tackle Jalen Travis, Bernhard Raimann is in concussion protocol, and linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither is on IR. That helps Houston's second-ranked sack defense win the game early. On his side, Marvin Harrison Jr. is out, which concentrates targets on Collins, Noel, Boutte and Schultz. Lead back Woody Marks is doubtful with a concussion, which weakens a run game that already ranks 24th in EPA.

keyMatchups.title: Shot plays vs leaky explosives
keyMatchups.body: Indy allows explosive passes at nearly the league's worst rate, and his 20+ yard throws are his most valuable. If either Colts corner sits, the windows widen further. This matchup is the one that produces his ceiling game.

keyMatchups.title: Tight end and slot targets
keyMatchups.body: Opposing TE1s and WR3s have produced well above their usual output against Indy. Schultz and the efficient secondary receivers look like his best routes to efficiency. Throws to the opponent's WR2 have been the stingiest matchup in the league.

keyMatchups.title: Blowout script caps volume
keyMatchups.body: With a double-digit spread and the league's worst passing offense on the other side, Houston could be running out the clock by the fourth quarter. Teams already lean on the run against Indy, which limits his attempts even in a good game.

nextGame.watch: Whether Gardner and Ward suit up. If either sits on the short week, Stroud's deep shots get a lot easier.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation is solid. He has an aggressive, downfield-first approach backed by real deep accuracy, protection that ranks near the top of the league, and a passing offense that ranks 7th in EPA. That should keep him a top-10-type yardage producer with above-average efficiency. What regresses is the scoring. A red-zone completion rate this far above expectation and a recent TD rate near 10% will not last. Expect something like 1.6 to 2.4 touchdowns a game rather than the three-plus of late, and a few more interceptions as the INT rate drifts up toward what his window-throwing invites.

Volume depends on script and health. Houston's poor run game keeps the ball in his hands, but favored spots like this week can cut his attempts. Harrison's hamstring and how the targets are redistributed will matter too. Moving looks from Hutchinson toward Noel and Boutte would lift his per-play numbers more than anything he changes himself.
swingFactors: Whether the deep ball keeps landing at this rate
Target distribution toward Noel/Boutte vs Hutchinson
Offensive line health sustaining low sack rates

confidence.note: Nine starts with a clear process change, but TD and INT rates sit on small, noisy samples.
